body.heading: Palms together
paragraphs: In India and Nepal, a common greeting presses the palms together with a slight bow and the word “Namaste” — often understood as a respectful recognition of the other person. In Thailand, a similar gesture, the wai, adjusts its height with the respect owed, and in Cambodia and Laos cousins of the gesture appear too.
What these share is a greeting that makes a small bow of the whole body: I arrive peacefully, and I honour you.

body.heading: Bows, hands, and hearts
paragraphs: In Japan, bowing carries the greeting, with deeper bows for deeper respect. In much of the Middle East and Central Asia, a hand placed over the heart after a handshake — or instead of one — adds sincerity to the words. Handshakes themselves, now global, began as a way of showing an empty, weaponless hand.
None of these is merely decoration. Each is a tiny ceremony that converts a stranger into a person, in under three seconds.

body.heading: Borrow respectfully
paragraphs: Travellers do well to follow the local lead: return a bow with a bow, accept the offered hand or the offered palm-press, and let your host set the form. Getting it slightly wrong with obvious goodwill is forgiven almost everywhere; not trying is remembered too.
And your own greeting, offered warmly and by name where you can, is part of the same worldwide language. The forms differ. The sentence underneath is always: you are worth greeting properly.

takeaway: Every greeting, in every form, makes the same small promise: you are worth greeting properly.
